source.title: Decomposing The Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Joshua Engels; L. Smith; Max Tegmark

page_placements.theme: Residual magnitudes and components are predictable

record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures SAE error vectors, their scaling across SAE sizes, and the effects of error components on downstream loss.
record.gate_note: The cited result that SAE errors are pathological relative to random perturbations comes from prior work and is not tested here. The paper's own results about linear prediction, scaling, component training, and downstream loss are recorded below.
record.test_reason: This is the original source for the claim. It directly measures linear predictability of SAE error, per-token error scaling across widths, and the properties and downstream loss contribution of linear vs nonlinear error. No verdict labels are given because it is the original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAE error is structured and predictable: about half of the error vector and over 90% of its norm are linearly predictable. Larger SAEs fail on the same tokens. Nonlinear error stays roughly constant at fixed sparsity, contains fewer unlearned features, and contributes proportionally to loss. They argue scaling alone may not remove it and that SAEs should be made 'better, not just bigger'.
record.recipe_differences: This is the original study. It examines TopK and JumpReLU SAE error using linear probes, cross-size per-token error prediction, and downstream interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Error-vector predictability varies with SAE width and L0. Error-norm predictability varies by layer, rising in middle layers and falling in the last layers; it is also lower for sparser and wider SAEs in the reported sweeps. Nonlinear FVU is approximately constant with width at fixed L0 in middle layers, while some other layers show a slight decrease.

fits_no_version.finding: 70–95% of the variance in squared SAE error norm is linearly predictable from the activation. R² dips in early and final layers and beats token-identity and other baselines.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE error norms are linearly predictable from input activations.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE outputs of the layer-19 attention and MLP components predict 4–14% of nonlinear error and up to about 10% of total error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some SAE error can be predicted from SAE outputs of adjacent model components.

record.problems: The main experiments use about 247k activations from 300 Pile contexts. Several scaling and component results are presented in figures without exact values in the text. The claim that nonlinear FVU remains constant at still larger widths is an extrapolation. The paper notes that results for some additional layers are uncertain because of sparse SAE coverage.

untested.parts: Entire version. The pathological-vs-random-error result is cited from Gurnee (2024) and not re-tested here.
Loss of circuit or steering behaviour when the error term is dropped.
Alternative sparsity penalties, dead-latent fixes, new architectures and end-to-end training. Only inference-time gradient pursuit is tested.
Persistence of error at widths beyond 1m. Cross-size prediction is shown only for Gemma 2 9B layer 20.
Direct identification that the linear error consists of specific unlearned features in real activations. This is supported only via a synthetic setup (Appendix C.3).

missing.what: Power-law fit of FVU with width asymptotes above the nonlinear floor, implying error does not vanish with scale (FVU 0.186 asymptote).
Feature-shrinkage check: cosine of linear error prediction with x is about 0.5, so b* is not merely reversing shrinkage.
Adding nonlinear error norm improves cross-size per-token error prediction by up to 5% FVU decrease.
Synthetic validation: estimated Dense correlates 0.98 with x′ noise; estimated Introduced correlates 0.90 with Sae(x′) noise.
Error-vector predictability across layers and models, and the L0/width dependence in additional layers.

record.verdict_notes: No supports/limits/challenges labels are given because this study is the original source for the claim. The reader's V3 'not_tested' is correct; the pathology result is cited from prior work. Experiments use Gemma Scope and Llama Scope SAEs on about 247k Pile activations; the component analyses use Gemma 2 9B layer 20 only.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures linear prediction of SAE error vectors, but does not establish that the predicted component consists specifically of features the SAE has not learned.
Persistence at still larger, untested SAE sizes is hypothesized from observed trends, not demonstrated.
No comparison is made between SAE reconstruction interventions and random errors of the same size.
The study does not establish that nonlinear error is fundamentally resistant to all further dictionary learning.
The study measures downstream cross-entropy effects, not loss of specific circuits or steering behaviours.
The study tests inference-time gradient pursuit, but not alternative sparsity penalties, dead-latent interventions, or end-to-end training.

rows.subject: all tested models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit an optimal linear transformation from input activations to SAE error vectors and report R².

conditions.value: TopK and JumpReLU suites; combinations of width, L0, layer, and model

rows.measure: R² predicting SAE error vector from input activation
rows.note: The reported range spans the tested combinations; the authors describe the values as higher than expected.
rows.check: State should be observed, not partial. R² of 15–72% is what V1 describes; the abstract says 'about half of the error vector', and the authors call it much higher than expected. The range spans Gemma Scope SAEs, with R² lower for wider and higher-L0 SAEs.

rows.subject: all tested models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a linear probe from input activations to squared SAE error norm.

conditions.value: combinations of width, L0, layer, and model

rows.note: This measures predictability of error norms from activations, not linear predictability of the error vector itself.
rows.check: This measures predicting the error norm from the activation, not norm prediction across SAE sizes (V2) or the error vector (V1). Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Predict larger-SAEs' per-token error norms from smaller-SAEs' per-token error norms using a scalar fit.
rows.measure: R² for per-token error-norm prediction between SAE sizes
rows.value: The paper describes prediction as highly predictable overall; accuracy decreases as SAEs get farther apart in scale.
rows.note: The figure plots the results, and the text describes the trend without giving exact R² values.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Compare per-token norms of linear and nonlinear error components across SAE widths.
rows.measure: Per-token norms of linearly predictable and nonlinearly predictable error
rows.value: Linear error norm decreases with SAE width; nonlinear error norm stays mostly constant.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes the plotted per-token pattern.
rows.check: Per-token nonlinear error staying constant with width also bears on V4's claim that the nonlinear part resists further dictionary learning. Only Gemma 2 9B layer 20 is shown, on 100 tokens.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix A.4; Figure 12; Section 4.4 and Figure 5 identify the tokens and setting.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Track nonlinear FVU across SAE widths at approximately fixed sparsity.
rows.note: The authors hypothesize that this trend continues at larger widths; that extrapolation is not directly tested.
rows.check: Also bears on V4. It holds for middle layers only; in other layers FVUnonlinear decreases slightly with width (Appendix A.2). Persistence at larger widths is extrapolated.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Apply the norm-prediction test to SAE error, linear error, and nonlinear error components.
rows.measure: R² of linear prediction of component norm from activations
rows.baseline: SAE error and linear error components
rows.value: Nonlinear error has a notably lower score than linear error.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as evidence that nonlinear error contains fewer not-yet-learned linear features.
rows.check: Should be observed: nonlinear error has notably lower norm-prediction R² across 329 SAEs, as V4 predicts. Subject is all tested SAEs (Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 2 9B, Llama Scope), not only a 16k Gemma 9B SAE. No exact values are given; the evidence is a figure (violin plot).

source_check.correct: The reported component-norm comparison pools 329 SAEs: Gemma 2 2B layer 12, Gemma 2 9B layer 20, Gemma Scope SAEs across layers with L0 closest to 60, and all tested Llama Scope SAEs. It is not restricted to one 16k-latent Gemma 2 9B layer-20 SAE.
source_check.problem: The subject and conditions describe the single-source retraining experiment rather than the pooled norm-prediction experiment; the pack's verdict fix identifies this correctly.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Train separate SAEs on linear and nonlinear components of a source SAE's error.
rows.measure: Fraction of variance unexplained by the newly trained SAE
rows.note: The nonlinear-error SAE has an absolute 5 percentage-point higher FVU.
rows.check: The gap is modest: FVU 0.59 vs 0.54 for a single source SAE. The baseline and value fields are fine.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.size_stated: SAEs trained on components of a 16k-latent SAE's error
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate feature explanations from SAEs trained on linear and nonlinear error using an automated interpretability procedure.
rows.measure: Automated interpretability accuracy across activation deciles
rows.value: SAE trained on linear error is about an absolute 5% more interpretable across deciles.
rows.note: The 5% difference is reported in the text; figure shows the decile results.
rows.check: The roughly 5% interpretability gap is modest and comes from a single source SAE, with a Llama 3.1 70B judge.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.size_stated: SAEs with width 16k or L0 approximately 60
rows.operation_detail: Insert SAE reconstruction plus linear error into the model in place of the original activation.

conditions.value: all tested width-16k or L0 approximately 60 SAEs

rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss recovered relative to inserting the SAE reconstruction alone and the normal forward pass
rows.value: The linear error component contributes proportionally to its size to the downstream cross-entropy increase; possibly slightly more than expected.
rows.note: The text describes the result; the plotted values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: This shows error components carry downstream cross-entropy effect in proportion to their size; it does not test circuits or steering. Gemma 2 9B layer 20 only.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.size_stated: SAEs with width 16k or L0 approximately 60
rows.operation_detail: Insert SAE reconstruction plus nonlinear error into the model in place of the original activation.

conditions.value: all tested width-16k or L0 approximately 60 SAEs

rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss recovered relative to inserting the SAE reconstruction alone and the normal forward pass
rows.value: The nonlinear error component contributes proportionally to its size to the downstream cross-entropy increase.
rows.note: The text describes the result; the plotted values are not stated numerically.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Apply inference-time gradient pursuit to a frozen SAE decoder, keeping L0 equal to the original SAE's L0.
rows.value: Total FVU decreases by 3 to 5%; nonlinear FVU stays almost constant.
rows.note: The intervention improves total reconstruction but does not materially reduce the nonlinear component.
rows.check: A better encoder (inference-time optimization) reduces total FVU by only 3–5% and leaves nonlinear FVU almost unchanged. So the dark matter does not shrink under this change to the SAE. Role should be main, not comparator.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Regress error components of the layer-20 residual SAE from SAE outputs for preceding model components.
rows.measure: R² predicting nonlinear error from preceding-component SAE outputs
rows.value: Previous model components predict between 4% and 14% of nonlinear error.
rows.note: This shows some predictability from other component outputs; it is not a direct test of further dictionary learning.
rows.check: Predicting error from SAEs of adjacent components does not measure any version; it is already listed in fits_no_version.

relation.reason: Its own experiments directly measure error-vector predictability, per-token scaling and differences between linear and nonlinear error.

tranche.reason: Original study directly establishes the linear-probe, cross-size prediction and component-comparison methods and measures.

source_check.notes: Checks cover this study only; other studies and synthesis counts were not independently verified. The authors' summary needs the middle-layer qualification for constant nonlinear error; Appendix A.2 describes decreases elsewhere as uncertain because SAE coverage is sparse.

statements.correction: Section 5.1 and Figure 6: component-norm prediction pooled across 329 SAEs, including Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 2 9B and Llama Scope; nonlinear-error norms less predictable than linear-error norms.
statements.problem: The component distinction is reported, but its pooled result is assigned to the single-source Gemma 2 9B layer-20 setting.

statements.correction: Sections 4 and 5.1; Figure 6: norm-predictability separation includes Llama 3.1 8B as well as Gemma 2 2B and 9B. Section 5.2: component retraining uses one Gemma 2 9B layer-20 source SAE. No explicit training-stage comparison.
statements.problem: The blanket Gemma-only restriction overlooks the component-norm comparison on Llama Scope SAEs. Component retraining and width-dependent component scaling remain Gemma experiments.

statements.correction: Section 5.1: component-norm predictability evaluated across 329 SAEs, including Llama 3.1 8B. Component scaling and component retraining reported on Gemma; tested model sizes remain within 1–10B.
statements.problem: The original's measured component separation is not entirely restricted to Gemma: its pooled norm-prediction experiment includes Llama Scope.
